chicken-breast-baked-broiled-or-roasted-.title: Chicken breast, baked, broiled, or roasted with marinade, skin not eaten

content.title: About
content.content: Skinless chicken breast is a lean source of protein prepared by baking, broiling, or roasting with a flavorful marinade. Cooking without the skin keeps the meat tender while reducing fat content. It is widely used in low‑fat diets, salads, quick‑cook meals, and various world cuisines.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chicken breast provides about 31 g of protein per 100 g, making it one of the most protein‑dense meat cuts.
Marinades often contain lemon juice, herbs, spices, and a small amount of oil, which enhance flavor and juiciness.
When baked or grilled without skin, the finished product typically contains less than 3 g of fat per 100 g.
Chicken breast is a staple in sports nutrition because of its high protein and low calorie profile.
In Hungarian cuisine, chicken breast is commonly used in "paprikash," a stew flavored with sweet paprika.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: Protein is essential for muscle growth, repair, and immune function.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Skinless breast contains very little saturated fat, supporting heart health.

items.title: B vitamins
items.content: It provides niacin (B3) and vitamin B6, which are important for energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Chicken breast supplies phosphorus, selenium, and zinc, vital for bones and antioxidant protection.

items.title: Weight‑management support
items.content: High protein and low calorie content help promote satiety and aid weight control.

items.title: Food‑borne illness risk
items.content: Undercooked chicken may harbor pathogens such as Salmonella. Cook to an internal temperature of 74 °C (165 °F).

items.title: Chicken allergy
items.content: Although uncommon, some individuals may be allergic to chicken proteins.

items.title: Sodium in marinades
items.content: Marinades can be high in salt; choose low‑sodium versions if you need to limit sodium intake.

items.title: Nutrient loss with overcooking
items.content: Excessive heat can degrade B‑vitamins.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice cooked breast for salads, add to sandwiches, stir‑fries, rice or vegetable dishes, or serve as a main course with a side. It pairs well with lemon, garlic, herbs, and light sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep raw breast refrigerated at 0‑4 °C for up to 2 days. Store cooked breast in an airtight container in the fridge for up to 3 days or freeze for up to 3 months. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or slimy texture.

content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated iced latte is a cold beverage made from espresso, milk, and ice, using beans that have had most of their caffeine removed. It retains the characteristic aroma and flavor of a classic latte while lacking the stimulating effect of caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Decaffeination is usually performed by water or CO₂ methods, preserving most flavor compounds.
Decaf iced latte is popular among people who avoid caffeine for medical reasons or sensitivity.
Sugar content depends on added syrups; many versions use sweeteners to balance bitterness.
Serving cold enhances perceived sweetness and aroma, making the drink especially refreshing in warm weather.
In some countries decaffeinated coffee is classified as a separate product category with its own quality standards.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Decaffeinated beans retain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports hydration
items.content: The high water and milk content of the drink contributes to overall fluid balance.

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Milk provides a good source of calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Low caffeine content
items.content: Suitable for individuals who need to limit caffeine but still want the coffee taste.

items.title: Provides vitamin B2
items.content: Riboflavin present in milk and coffee participates in energy metabolism.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: People with lactose intolerance or milk allergy should opt for plant‑based milk alternatives.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Added syrups can increase calories and affect blood glucose levels.

items.title: Loss of some aromatic compounds
items.content: The decaffeination process may reduce certain flavor molecules, making the taste less intense.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the decaf iced latte chilled over ice; optionally add flavored syrups, vanilla, or a sprinkle of cinnamon. Plant‑based milks (almond, oat) can be used for a vegan version.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the prepared drink in the refrigerator for up to 24 hours. Keep decaffeinated coffee beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place.

content.title: About
content.content: Cress (Lepidium sativum) is an annual herb cultivated for its edible leaves and stems. It has bright green foliage, a mildly peppery taste, and a crunchy texture. Cress is usually eaten raw in salads, sandwiches, soups, and as a garnish.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Cress belongs to the Brassicaceae family and is closely related to radish and mustard.
It germinates quickly: seedlings appear within 3–5 days after sowing.
Cress is often used in culinary shows as a "living" garnish because the leaves keep growing after harvest.
Ancient cultures used cress as a medicinal herb for colds and digestive issues.
Cress seeds are rich in glucosinolates, which give a characteristic mustard-like aroma when the plant is cut.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C
items.content: Cress provides a high amount of vitamin C, supporting the immune system and acting as an antioxidant.

items.title: Source of vitamins K and A
items.content: Vitamin K is essential for blood clotting, while vitamin A supports vision and skin health.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: Cress supplies calcium, iron, and magnesium, important for bones, blood formation, and nerve function.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: One cup of fresh cress contains fewer than 30 calories, making it a great addition to weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: The fiber in cress promotes regular bowel movements and may help relieve constipation.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cress, such as itching, swelling, or rash.

items.title: Bacterial contamination
items.content: Raw leaves can be contaminated with Salmonella or E. coli; thorough washing before consumption is recommended.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: High amounts of vitamin K may affect the efficacy of anticoagulants like warfarin.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Add cress to fresh salads, sandwiches, soups, omelets, and smoothies. It can be used as a garnish or mixed with other herbs. Before eating, rinse the leaves well under running water.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cress in the refrigerator in an airtight container or a bag with a damp paper towel. It stays fresh for 3–5 days. Discard if leaves turn yellow, develop a sour smell, or become limp.
